items.title: UK adds 13 designations and 6 specifications under the Russia sanctions regime
items.summary: On 6 August 2026 the UK Sanctions List was updated with 13 new designations and 6 new specifications under the Russia regime, the latest in a steady run of additions through July and August.
items.whyItMatters: Banks with a UK nexus should refresh sanctions screening lists to capture the new Russia-regime designations and specifications promptly, to avoid processing transactions for newly listed persons or entities.

sources.name: UK Sanctions List

items.title: HMRC names and fines Petrofac Facilities Management for Russia sanctions breaches
items.summary: HMRC publicly named Petrofac Facilities Management Limited (PFML) on 29 June 2026 after it accepted a £569,157 compound settlement for supplying sanctioned industrial goods and technical assistance to Russia-connected individuals during 2022-2023, while winding down its Russian operations. It is the first time HMRC has publicly named a firm accepting this type of settlement.
items.whyItMatters: The public naming signals a new HMRC enforcement posture for strategic-export and sanctions violations; banks financing or servicing exporters winding down Russia-exposed operations should reassess due-diligence expectations around self-reporting and technical-assistance exposure.

sources.name: HMRC: Energy firm named after £500,000 Russia sanctions settlement

items.title: OFSI's Lukoil wind-down licences approach expiry in August 2026
items.summary: OFSI's general licences permitting continued business with Lukoil International entities (INT/2025/8031092, extended to 25 August 2026) and Lukoil Bulgaria entities (INT/2025/7895596, extended to 13 August 2026) are both due to lapse this month; the international-entities licence was also amended to remove the frozen-account payment restriction in paragraph 4.2. (Confidence: medium — corroborated via legal-sector reporting on the licence text rather than a direct read of the licence document itself.)
items.whyItMatters: Banks with counterparties relying on these licences to continue Lukoil-linked business need to confirm wind-down completion or a further extension before the licences lapse, or transactions risk falling outside authorised activity.

sources.name: OFSI General Licences

items.title: OTSI publishes guidance on banknote sanctions with Russia and Belarus
items.summary: On 3 August 2026 OTSI published guidance on complying with sanctions relating to banknotes, covering the prohibition on providing banknotes to persons connected with Russia or Belarus (including postal and hand-carried transfers), with a £10,000 personal-travel exception.
items.whyItMatters: Retail and private banking teams handling customer cash withdrawals or currency exchange tied to travel to Russia or Belarus should align controls with the new £10,000 personal-use threshold and the guidance's due-diligence expectations.

sources.name: OTSI: Complying with sanctions relating to banknotes

items.title: OFAC designates Iran-linked individuals and issues amended Iran FAQ
items.summary: On 7 August 2026 OFAC added Iran-related and counter-terrorism designations to the SDN list, including Saeed Ghasempour and Amir Hendi, removed certain counter-narcotics designations, and issued an amended Iran-related FAQ (FAQ 1257). (Confidence: medium — the full designee list and the FAQ's substance were not independently confirmed beyond the two individuals identified.)
items.whyItMatters: US-nexus banks should refresh OFAC screening lists for the new Iran-related SDN entries and review amended FAQ 1257 for any change to permitted-activity guidance.
entities: Saeed Ghasempour (also known as Sa'id Ghasempur)

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions

items.title: OFAC sanctions crypto exchanges and a front-company network tied to Iran's IRGC
items.summary: On 7 August 2026 OFAC sanctioned seven entities and five individuals, including two UAE-based exchange houses, for helping Iran's banking system move hundreds of millions of dollars and supporting the IRGC, including alleged support for Shahr Bank's efforts to repatriate oil-sale revenue.
items.whyItMatters: Digital-asset and correspondent-banking teams should screen counterparties against the newly designated exchange houses and front companies, and reassess exposure to UAE-based crypto exchanges used in Iran-linked flows.

sources.name: US Treasury: Treasury Sanctions Crypto Exchanges Funding Iran's IRGC and Enabling Illicit Finance

items.title: OFAC removes 84 SDN entries and updates 22 more in second modernization round
items.summary: On 27 July 2026 OFAC completed the second round of its sanctions-list modernization initiative (announced by the Treasury Secretary in May 2026), removing 84 individuals and entities, primarily deceased persons, defunct entities and decades-old listings, improving identifying data on 22 entries, and consolidating 18 duplicate entries.
items.whyItMatters: Screening teams should reconcile watchlists against the delisted and consolidated entries so false-positive alerts on outdated SDN records are cleared, and confirm no active relationships were incorrectly blocked against superseded entries.

sources.name: US Treasury: Treasury Announces Second Round of Sanctions Removals, Updates in Modernization Initiative

items.title: OFAC settles Iran sanctions case with Rice Lake Weighing Systems for $60,764
items.summary: On 12 August 2026 OFAC announced a $60,764 settlement with Wisconsin-based Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. over eight apparent violations: its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to a UAE distributor between July 2019 and November 2021 knowing the goods would be re-exported to an end-user in Iran.
items.whyItMatters: A reminder that OFAC enforcement reaches indirect re-export exposure through foreign subsidiaries; trade-finance teams should verify end-use and re-export controls for goods routed through UAE intermediaries toward Iran.

sources.name: OFAC: Settlement Agreement with Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc.

items.title: EU adopts 21st sanctions package against Russia, its largest listing round yet
items.summary: On 23 July 2026 the Council of the EU adopted its 21st sanctions package against Russia: 218 additional listings (48 individuals, 170 entities), the highest number since the war began. From 13 August 2026, transaction bans extend to 33 more Russian financial institutions plus banks in Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia and India; from 25 August 2026, Russian nationals are barred from sitting on the boards of any EU crypto-asset services business. The package also expands energy, trade and military-industrial restrictions.
items.whyItMatters: The 13 and 25 August transaction-ban and crypto-board effective dates give banks a narrow window to unwind or restructure relationships with the newly listed financial institutions and crypto-asset businesses before the prohibitions take effect.

sources.name: European Commission: EU adopts 21st package of sanctions against Russia
Council of the EU: 21st package of sanctions

items.title: UN 1267 Committee amends the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
items.summary: On 13 August 2026 the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) enacted amendments to entries on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List (asset freeze, travel ban and arms embargo). (Confidence: low — which specific entries were amended could not be confirmed: main.un.org and press.un.org both blocked automated access during this run, so this item rests on secondary search corroboration rather than the primary notice.)
items.whyItMatters: Any amendment to the 1267 list can affect identifying details on existing screening matches; banks should pull the current ISIL/Al-Qaida list rather than rely on cached data until the specific change is confirmed.

sources.name: UN Security Council: Sanctions List Materials (1267 Committee)

items.title: UK adds 6 new designations under the Global Human Rights and Counter-Terrorism regimes
items.summary: On 8 August 2026 the UK Sanctions List was updated with 5 new designations under the Global Human Rights regime and 1 new designation under the Counter-Terrorism (International) regime, according to the list's published change log. The Global Human Rights regime entries were further varied on 9 September and corrected on 10 September; the change log does not name the individuals or entities involved.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should refresh Global Human Rights and Counter-Terrorism (International) regime screening lists to capture the new designations and the follow-up variation/correction made in the days after.

sources.name: UK Sanctions List

items.title: UK amends 21 entries on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaeda sanctions list
items.summary: On 20 August 2026 the UK Sanctions List recorded 21 variations to entries under the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaeda regime, the largest of several amendments to this regime in the period — 4 further variations were made on 17 August, 1 on 7 September, and 1 correction on 10 September. The published change log gives counts only, not which entries or individuals were affected. (Confidence: medium — the specific entries changed were not independently confirmed beyond the change-log counts.)
items.whyItMatters: Any amendment to this regime's entries can affect identifying details on existing screening matches; banks should pull the current ISIL/Al-Qaeda list rather than rely on cached data.

sources.name: UK Sanctions List

items.title: UK makes further Russia regime amendments, including one revocation, plus minor Afghanistan regime changes
items.summary: Between 27 August and 21 September 2026 the UK Sanctions List recorded a further run of amendments: 2 variations under the Afghanistan regime (27 August), 1 more (28 August), 4 amendments under the Russia regime (2 September), 1 amendment (3 September), 1 variation (10 September), 1 variation (11 September), and 1 revocation — a de-listing — under the Russia regime (21 September). The published change log gives counts only, not which entries or individuals were affected.
items.whyItMatters: The 21 September revocation is a de-listing that should be reflected in screening records promptly; the other entries are amendments to existing listings that may affect identifying details on current screening matches.

sources.name: UK Sanctions List

items.title: OTSI publishes its Annual Review for 2025-26
items.summary: On 28 August 2026 the Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation (OTSI) published its Annual Review for the 2025-26 financial year, covering compliance engagement, licensing and enforcement activity, with the Russia sanctions regime as a key focus. The review highlights the implementation of new Sanctions End-Use Controls in May 2026 and the expansion of OTSI's licensing remit in April 2026 to cover exports of sanctioned goods and ancillary services, in addition to its existing remit over sanctioned services.
items.whyItMatters: OTSI's expanded remit — now covering licensing for sanctioned goods exports, not just services — and the new End-Use Controls change what trade-sanctions compliance teams need to screen and license for; worth reviewing current processes against the updated scope.

sources.name: OTSI Blog: Annual Review 2025-2026

items.title: UK lays major Iran sanctions amendment regulations, in force 29 September 2026
items.summary: The Iran (Sanctions) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/983), made on 7 September 2026, substantially expand the UK's Iran sanctions regime and come into force on 29 September 2026. New provisions include financial-sector prohibitions on lending, correspondent banking, insurance and dealing in Iranian government-guaranteed bonds issued after 8 September 2026; new trade prohibitions on gold, precious metals, diamonds, energy-related goods and technology, and sectoral software; new banknote-export and oil-tanker-related prohibitions; and new ship and aircraft measures including UK port-entry and landing restrictions for Iran-connected vessels and aircraft.
items.whyItMatters: This is a broad expansion of the Iran sanctions framework spanning financial services, trade and shipping/aviation; banks should review Iran-connected lending, correspondent banking, insurance, bond, trade-finance and vessel-related exposure against the new prohibitions before they take effect on 29 September 2026.

sources.name: The Iran (Sanctions) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/983)

items.title: US removes Syria's State Sponsor of Terrorism designation and delists HTS
items.summary: On 24 August 2026 the US State Department removed Syria's designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism, lifting prohibitions under the Terrorism List Governments Sanctions Regulations. The State Department also revoked Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham's (HTS, formerly al-Nusrah Front) designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organisation, and OFAC removed HTS from the SDN List and revoked the related Syria General License 25 as no longer necessary. Commerce, State and Treasury issued an updated Tri-Seal Advisory on Syria sanctions and export-control relief.
items.whyItMatters: This substantially changes the Syria sanctions landscape; banks with restricted or heightened-scrutiny policies tied to Syria's former SST status or to HTS/Syrian-government links should reassess those policies and screening rules, including reliance on the now-revoked Syria GL 25.

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Removal of Syria's designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism

items.title: OFAC designates a large Iran-linked network of individuals, shipping and front companies
items.summary: On 24 August 2026, alongside the Syria/HTS action, OFAC added numerous individuals and entities to the SDN List under Iran-related sanctions authorities (including E.O. 13846, E.O. 13902 and the Iran-related non-proliferation authority), spanning Iran-based cyber actors, senior Iranian figures including Amir Hatami and Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, and a Turkey/UAE/Hong Kong/Singapore/China network of shipping and trading companies including Good Luck Shipping LLC and Amdeh Ship Management and Operation Co. L.L.C. OFAC also published a new E.O. 13902 sectoral determination covering aviation, digital-asset, gold, shipping and technology sectors of the Iranian economy, suspended Iran General Licenses F and G, and issued new Iran General Licenses AA and BB.
items.whyItMatters: The scale and geographic spread of this round (UAE, Hong Kong, Singapore, China, Turkey) means correspondent-banking and trade-finance teams with counterparties in those jurisdictions should screen against the new SDN entries, particularly shipping and trading front companies, and review use of the now-suspended Iran GLs F and G.
entities: Amdeh Ship Management and Operation Co. L.L.C.

items.title: OFAC delists Ethiopia sanctions program participants as underlying national emergency expires
items.summary: The national emergency declared in Executive Order 14046 (September 2021), concerning the humanitarian and human rights crisis in Ethiopia, has expired. On 18 September 2026 OFAC removed from the SDN List the individuals and entities designated under that programme — including the People's Front for Democracy and Justice, the Eritrean Defense Forces, Red Sea Trading Corporation and Hidri Trust — and removed the programme's FAQs from its website.
items.whyItMatters: Ethiopia/Eritrea (E.O. 14046) sanctions screening flags should be retired for the delisted parties; banks maintaining blocked-property records tied to this programme should confirm the delisting before continuing to treat these parties as blocked.
entities: People's Front for Democracy and Justice

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Expiration of Emergency With Respect to the Situation in Ethiopia

items.title: OFAC issues general licence authorising negotiations for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH
items.summary: On 18 September 2026 OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131J, authorising certain transactions for the negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities, alongside two amended Russia-related FAQs (1224 and 1225).
items.whyItMatters: This is a US-side counterpart to the Lukoil wind-down activity already being tracked on the UK side (OFSI's Lukoil general licences); banks with Lukoil International-linked exposure should review GL 131J's scope before relying on it for sale-related transactions.

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Issuance of Amended Russia-related General License

items.title: OFAC tightens Iran licensing policy and settles $1.43m Iran sanctions case under Operation Economic Outcast
items.summary: On 10 September 2026 OFAC modified its Iran-related specific-licensing policy to a presumption of denial, with narrow exceptions (e.g. risk to life, limb or environmental safety), as part of Operation Economic Outcast. Separately, OFAC announced a $1,427,230 settlement with an individual who provided management-consulting and advisory services to a leading Iranian software company, received Iranian-origin dividends into US bank accounts, and acquired Iranian real property; OFAC found the apparent violations egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed.
items.whyItMatters: Teams handling Iran-related specific-licence applications should expect a presumption of denial going forward; the settlement is a reminder that indirect Iran exposure through consulting services, dividend receipts and real-property acquisition falls within OFAC's enforcement scope.

sources.name: OFAC Recent Actions: Licensing Policy Update and Settlement Agreement

items.title: OFAC designates Kata'ib Hizballah and Hizballah-linked financial networks in Iraq, Lebanon and the UAE
items.summary: On 10 September 2026 OFAC added individuals and entities to the SDN List linked to Kata'ib Hizballah in Iraq and a Hizballah financial network in Lebanon, including exchange houses and general-trading companies — Shams and Bahr Trading Company L.L.C. (Dubai), Gold Pro SARL (Beirut), Yousef Ibrahim Mansour and Partner for Exchange (Lebanon), and Ain Al Iraq for Protection Systems Technology and Audio, Visual, and Communications Solutions Company Ltd (Baghdad) — under the Hizballah Financial Sanctions Regulations and related counter-terrorism authorities.
items.whyItMatters: Correspondent-banking and trade-finance teams with Iraq, Lebanon or UAE exposure should screen against the new entries, particularly exchange houses and general-trading companies used as Hizballah-linked financial conduits.

items.title: OFAC designates VTB Bank, one of Russia's largest banks, for Iran sanctions evasion
items.summary: On 14 September 2026, under Operation Economic Outcast, OFAC designated VTB Bank Public Joint Stock Company — one of Russia's largest financial institutions — pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Treasury said VTB Bank opened offices in Iran, established correspondent banking relationships with sanctioned Iranian banks, moved billions in frozen Iranian assets, and built a rial/ruble settlement system to expand bilateral trade. VTB was previously designated under Russia-related authorities (E.O. 13662 in January 2025 and E.O. 14024 in February 2022).
items.whyItMatters: Foreign financial institutions that continue dealing with VTB Bank now face secondary sanctions risk under Iran authorities on top of existing Russia-related exposure; banks should confirm no correspondent or other relationships with VTB remain in place and review counterparties for indirect exposure.
entities: VTB Bank Public Joint Stock Company

items.title: OFAC designates BitBank and the Zanjani digital-asset network funding the IRGC
items.summary: On 17 September 2026 OFAC designated BitBank, an Iranian digital-asset exchange controlled by OFAC-designated financier Babak Zanjani, along with its developer Pishtaz Simorgh Electronic Trade Company and three Zanjani associates — Hossein Ali Zaker Hossein, Mohammad Mahdi Zaker Hossein and Seyed Adel Heidari — under E.O. 13902's digital-asset-sector authority. OFAC said BitBank was used since June 2026 to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars in Bitcoin to the IRGC on behalf of OFAC-designated Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority.
items.whyItMatters: Digital-asset and correspondent-banking teams should screen counterparties against BitBank and the newly designated Zanjani-network entities and individuals, and treat Iranian digital-asset exchanges generally as elevated sanctions-evasion risk per OFAC's guidance (FAQ 1250, FAQ 1257).

items.title: EU extends Ukraine territorial-integrity sanctions listings for three years, delists a handful of individuals
items.summary: On 22 September 2026 the Council of the EU prolonged the restrictive measures targeting those responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence for a further 36 months, until 22 September 2029. The listings apply to more than 3,000 individuals and entities. As part of the review, the Council decided not to renew the listings of three individuals and one entity, and removed three deceased persons from the list.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should update screening records for the delisted and non-renewed entries while continuing to treat the roughly 3,000 extended listings as in force through 2029.

sources.name: Council of the EU: Ukraine's territorial integrity: EU extends individual listings for three years

items.title: EU lists five more individuals over Russia's military-industrial complex
items.summary: On 7 August 2026 the Council of the EU adopted restrictive measures against five individuals holding senior positions at Russian defence and military-technology companies, including Ramil Nailevich Badgutdinov (General Director of JSC Serpukhov Plant Metallist, which produces components used in Russia's Iskander-M missile system) and Aleksandr Yurevich Dyukarev (General Director of JSC Krasnoyarsk Machine-Building Plant, which produces the RS-28 Sarmat missile system), plus directors of companies producing military communications systems and UAV/space-related military technology.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should screen for the newly listed individuals and review any exposure to the Russian defence-industrial companies they lead.

sources.name: Council of the EU: Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine: EU lists five additional individuals supporting Russia's military-industrial complex

items.title: EU sanctions Prince Holding Group, Jin Bei Group and DKBA over Southeast Asian scam centres
items.summary: On 30 July 2026 the Council of the EU imposed restrictive measures under its Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime on seven persons and three entities responsible for serious human rights violations tied to scam-centre operations in Cambodia and Myanmar, including human trafficking and torture of trafficked workers. Those listed include the Prince Holding Group and its chairman Chen Zhi, the Jin Bei Group and its chairman Zhu Zhongbiao, and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), a Burmese armed group that controls territory where scam-centre compounds operate.
items.whyItMatters: The Prince Holding Group's cryptocurrency investment-scam operations reach victims globally; correspondent-banking, payments and crypto-facing teams should screen for the newly listed entities and individuals.
items.programme: EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime

sources.name: Council of the EU: Scam centres in Southeast Asia: EU lists seven persons and three entities responsible for serious human rights violations

items.title: EU sanctions six more individuals over Iran human-rights violations
items.summary: On 24 July 2026 the Council of the EU sanctioned six additional individuals over serious human-rights violations in Iran: five judges of Iran's Revolutionary Courts who presided over trials of religious minorities and political dissidents — including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi — imposing death sentences, long prison terms and flogging; and Nima Salehi, an Iranian hacker and founder of the 'Ashiyane' cyber group linked to the IRGC and Iran's Cyber Police. The EU's Iran human-rights sanctions now cover 269 individuals and 53 entities.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should screen for the newly listed individuals under the EU's Iran human-rights sanctions regime.

sources.name: Council of the EU: Iran: Council sanctions an additional six individuals over serious human rights violations

items.title: UN 1267 Committee amends 21 entries on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
items.summary: On 18 August 2026 the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) amended 21 entries on the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List, updating identifying details on previously listed individuals. The changes include confirming Isnilon Totoni Hapilon (QDi.204) as killed in the Philippines in October 2017, and correcting aliases and other identifying details for entries including Nurjaman Riduan Isamuddin, also known as Hambali (QDi.087).
items.whyItMatters: Banks should refresh cached copies of the ISIL/Al-Qaida list to capture the updated identifying details, including death confirmations that may resolve stale screening matches.

sources.name: UN Security Council Press Release SC/16435

items.title: UN sanctions committees make further technical amendments to Taliban and ISIL/Al-Qaida list entries
items.summary: On 27 August 2026 the 1988 Committee (Taliban sanctions) amended one entry, updating identifying details for Abdul Salam Hanafi. On 4 September 2026 the 1267 Committee amended two ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida entries, updating identifying details for Sanaullah Ghafari (a.k.a. Shahab al Muhajir, leader of ISIL-Khorasan) and Abubakar Swalleh (an ISIL facilitator in East and Southern Africa). Both changes are identifying-detail corrections rather than new designations.
items.whyItMatters: Banks should refresh cached copies of the Taliban and ISIL/Al-Qaida lists to capture the updated identifying details on these existing entries.

items.title: Security Council adopts resolution 2828 on Sudan and South Sudan Secretary-General reporting
items.summary: The Security Council adopted resolution S/RES/2828 (2026) on 11 September 2026, titled "Reports of the Secretary-General on the Sudan and South Sudan", under the framework of the 1591 Sudan sanctions committee. (Confidence: low — the resolution's operative text was not accessible during this run, so whether or how it changes the Sudan sanctions measures themselves — arms embargo, asset freeze, travel ban or panel-of-experts mandate — could not be confirmed.)
items.whyItMatters: Banks with Sudan-related exposure should watch for a fuller readout of resolution 2828, since resolutions under the 1591 Committee framework can renew or adjust the Sudan sanctions regime's measures.
